items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I finally realized that everybody else that does arrangements of Monk‟s music tries to make it sound like Monk. I said I‟m not going to do that. I‟m going to try to make it sound like me, using Monk‟s music.

ctx.x: With the drummer he had at that time? Or just overall, as a concept?

Overall. He never did it while I was there, but guys told me that he had done it afterwards. We get so used to using our eyes to absorb music that we forget it‟s got – the ideal place is your ears. There‟s a story about Monk that somebody told me. He was doing a date with some horns. He‟d bring in a big case every day, set it over in the corner, go and sit at the piano, call the players over one by one, and have them learn their parts by ear. After they got everything recorded, they said, “Monk, did you really…
When you say his beat was different from anybody else, maybe a little more descriptive?

items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: was it the Kronos Quartet that did the Monk things?

ctx.x: Yeah. They’ve got a string section, it’s a fairly good size, it’s almost 30 strings, and they’re very enthusiastic and very cooperative. Most string players don’t want to hear about playing jazz. They don’t even like contemporary classical music. But these guys can actually swing a little bit. They can do two types the [scats] kind of swing, and the straight-eighth thing, which is a very subtle thing that a lot of horn players are not familiar with. But these guys do it and they volunteer to do it. Because I had…
Yeah. Turtle Island also. They swing pretty good. But you said something about straight eighth notes. How do you mean that? I assume that that is slightly different from Mozart eighth notes.
